units.meaning: Hereinafter, 'applicant' refers to the person whose citizenship and identity are subject to adjudication, which includes adjudications involving form DS-2060.

source_spans.quote: The term “applicant” is used hereinafter for the individual whose citizenship and identity is being adjudicated, including for form DS-2060.

units.meaning: Within this chapter, 'minor applicants' means un-emancipated individuals under 18 years of age.

source_spans.quote: For purposes of this chapter, minor applicants are defined as un-emancipated applicants under the age of 18.

units.meaning: Any name change that 8 FAM 403.1-5 does not define as immaterial constitutes a material discrepancy.

source_spans.quote: A material discrepancy is any name change that is not defined as immaterial in 8 FAM 403.1-5.

units.meaning: The applicant is required to provide an explanation for any material discrepancies existing between the name stated on the passport application and the name shown in the evidence of identity and evidence of U.S. citizenship or non-citizen U.S. nationality.

source_spans.quote: The applicant must explain any material discrepancies between the name on the application and the name recorded in the evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality and the evidence of identity (see 22 CFR 51.25).

units.meaning: Unless the married names exception in 8 FAM 403.1-4(C) applies, material discrepancies across the application name, citizenship/nationality evidence, or identity evidence must be documented by submitting at least one acceptable document listed in this section.

source_spans.quote: Material discrepancies between the name recorded on the application, the applicant's evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality, or the evidence of identity must be documented by submission of one or more of the documents listed in this section (see an exception for married names in 8 FAM 403.1-4(C)).

units.meaning: An applicant is prohibited from continuing to use a previous name following a material name change, unless the name change documentation expressly allows them to keep using that previous name.

source_spans.quote: The applicant may not continue to use a previous name after a material name change unless the name change documentation specifically permits the applicant to continue using that name (see 8 FAM 403.1-6 regarding “known as” names).

units.meaning: If an applicant applying on form DS-11 underwent a material name change more than one year before applying but did not update their ID to the new name, the application must be suspended to request an acceptable ID showing the new name.

source_spans.quote: If the applicant has had a material name change more than one year prior to applying on form DS-11 but has not updated her/his ID to reflect the material name change, you must suspend the application to request an acceptable ID in the new name.

units.meaning: When an applicant with an outdated ID from a name change more than one year before a DS-11 application faces urgent or emergency travel that leaves insufficient time to request and obtain acceptable ID, adjudicators may issue a limited-validity passport in the requested name.

source_spans.quote: If there is insufficient time to request that the applicant submit acceptable ID prior to urgent or emergency travel, a limited-validity passport may be issued in the requested name;

source_spans.quote: The applicant generally will need the name change documentation to change the name on her/his ID.

units.meaning: Before returning name change documentation to the applicant alongside an Information Request Letter (IRL), adjudicators must fully notate the documentation, including recording that it was 'seen and returned.'

source_spans.quote: You must fully notate the name change documentation prior to returning the documentation, including that the documentation was "seen and returned," to the applicant with the information request letter (IRL);

units.meaning: Applicants whose material name change took place within one year before applying on form DS-11 are exempt from submitting ID reflecting their new name.

source_spans.quote: Applicants who have had a material name change within one year of applying on a form DS-11 do not need to submit ID in the new name.

units.meaning: If an applicant whose material name change occurred within one year of applying on form DS-11 has not yet changed their ID, they are required to submit their name change documentation.

source_spans.quote: However, if the ID has not yet been changed, they must submit their name change documentation.

source_spans.quote:
8 FAM 403.1-3(B) Name Spacing

(CT:CITZ-96; 08-04-2023)

units.meaning: Pursuant to ICAO recommendations, all U.S. passports, Form FS-240, and Form DS-2060 are produced with text in all uppercase letters.

source_spans.quote: a. In accordance with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) recommendations, U.S. passports, form FS-240, and form DS-2060 are printed in all uppercase letters.

units.meaning: Explains the formatting reality that uppercase printing of multi-part names merges parts into a single word unless spaces are inserted between the parts.

source_spans.quote: Printing a name with multiple parts in uppercase letters causes the name to appear as one word unless the parts are separated with spaces.

units.meaning: Personnel are required to make a determination on how a multi-part name will appear on the issued document.

source_spans.quote: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multi-part name, personnel should add a space on the current application if the applicant's previous passport contained a space.

source_spans.quote: (1) If the applicant's previous passport had a space, you should add a space on the current application;
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multi-part name for an applicant lacking a previous passport, personnel should add a space on the current application if their citizenship/nationality evidence or ID has a space.

source_spans.quote: (2) If the applicant does not have a previous passport and the applicant's evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality or ID has a space, you should add a space on the current application; or
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When an applicant explicitly communicates a preference verbally or in writing to add or remove spacing in a multi-part name, personnel are permitted to add or remove spacing according to that preference.

source_spans.quote: (3) If the applicant expresses a clear preference to add or remove space, either verbally or in writing, you may add or remove it per the applicant's preference.
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: Personnel should maintain consistent spacing across last names when receiving applications from multiple family members, unless an individual family member explicitly indicates a clear preference for alternative spacing.

source_spans.quote: NOTE: If you receive applications from several family members, you should space the last names consistently, unless a family member expresses a clear preference for a different spacing.

units.meaning: On special-issuance passports, the last name spacing for an eligible family member should conform to the spacing used in the sponsor's last name.

source_spans.quote: NOTE: For special-issuance passports, the spacing of an eligible family member's last name should match the spacing of the last name of the sponsor.

units.meaning: Issues regarding name spacing generally do not justify rewriting a passport, except when the Department failed to honor the applicant's clearly expressed preference.

source_spans.quote: b. Name spacing issues are generally not sufficient cause to rewrite a passport, unless the Department disregarded the applicant's clear preference (see 8 FAM 1001.2).

units.meaning: Personnel are required to convert Arabic ordinal numbers in names into Roman numerals (such as converting 2nd to II, and 3rd to III).

source_spans.quote: c. Arabic ordinal numbers must be changed to Roman numerals, for example, 2nd to II, 3rd to III:

units.meaning: Notes that applicants may use the prefix 'Sr.' to represent the Spanish title 'Señor' rather than an English suffix.

source_spans.quote: d. Some applicants may include the prefix “Sr.” as an abbreviation for “Señor” in Spanish meaning “Mr.” or “Mister” in English.

units.meaning: If personnel determine that 'Sr.' is used as an abbreviation for 'Señor', they must follow the instructions governing ranks and titles in 8 FAM 403.1-5(C).

source_spans.quote: If you determine that this is the case, follow the guidance in 8 FAM 403.1-5(C) regarding ranks and titles.
d. Some applicants may include the prefix “Sr.” as an abbreviation for “Señor” in Spanish meaning “Mr.” or “Mister” in English.

units.meaning: Issues concerning name suffixes generally do not constitute sufficient reason to rewrite a passport, unless the Department failed to follow the applicant's clearly expressed preference.

source_spans.quote: e. Name suffix issues are generally not sufficient cause to rewrite a passport, unless the Department disregarded the applicant's clear preference (see 8 FAM 1001.2).
